To cause imperfection of vision in; to dim; to darken.
d.e: His eyes are blurred with the lightning's glare.

d.t: To sully; to stain; to blemish, as reputation.
d.e: Sarcasms may eclipse thine own, / But cannot blur my lost renown.

d.t: To transfer the input focus away from.
d.e: Then give this box focus to blur the first one: […]

d.t: To use a sign, image, expression, etc. sufficiently close to a trademarked one that it causes confusion between them.
A smear, smudge or blot.
Something that appears hazy or indistinct.
d.e: The surroundings went by in a blur.

d.t: Haziness, blurriness.
d.e: Unfortunately, a small artificial pupil also tends to increase the amount of diffraction somewhat, but this increase in blur is considerably smaller than the decrease that results from the control of other factors.

d.t: A moral stain or blot.
d.e: […]with her raillyng sette a great blurre on myne honesty

d.t: Lacking awareness; clueless or confused.
d.e: If a Singaporean gets frustrated at your stupidity, he can scold you for being blur as sotong (clueless as a squid).

d.t: A short description of a book, film, or other work, written and used for promotional purposes.
d.e: In a few weeks, blurbs would come back; a few, or many, depending on the book. There were certain writers we knew were always good for a blurb: Louis Untermeyer would always come through — poetry, fiction, humor — whatever, he'd send a well‐turned commendation.

d.t: To write or quote in a blurb.
d.e: When Rene Rodriguez of The Miami Herald blogged about having seen and loved “The Departed” in Toronto in a supposedly private screening last fall, Warner Brothers “scolded me very strongly,” he said, “but they still blurbed a line from my blog in their opening ad.”

d.t: To supply with a blurb.
d.e: The unseemly business of book blurbing has been source of both humor and concern in the pages of The New Yorker.

d.t: An explosive low-pitched sound resembling a burp.
d.e: It would start, then stall, then start again with a blurp, while clouds of blue smoke and sickening gas fumes polluted the air.

d.t: Out of focus; partially obscured; smudged.
d.e: blurred image

d.t: The characteristic of being blurry.
A blurry patch.
d.e: Several attempts were made to remove the blurrings in the tomograms.

d.t: Not clear, crisp, or focused; having fuzzy edges.
d.e: If I take off my glasses, everything close up looks blurry.

d.t: Not clear; lacking well-defined boundaries.
d.e: It would seem that the line between flirting and sexual harassment has become quite blurry.

d.t: [chiefly with out] To utter suddenly and unadvisedly; to speak quickly or without thought; to divulge inconsiderately.
d.e: Please think about your reply and don't just blurt out the first thing that comes to mind.

d.t: To spurt.
d.e: the sound of rusty water blurting from the faucet in the kitchen

d.t: An abrupt outburst.
Something that is blurted, or spoken hastily without thinking.
d.e: The school often has far more information than parents realise, e.g. from the blurtings of the child and his peers, the behaviour of the parents, and what the school bus driver has seen.

d.t: An act of blushing; a pink or red glow on the face caused by embarrassment, shame, shyness, love, etc.
d.e: Why, Warwick, canst thou speak against thy liege, Whom thou obeyed’st thirty and six years, And not bewray thy treason with a blush?

d.t: A glow; a flush of colour, especially pink or red.
d.e: And now the rosy blush of morn began to mantle in the east, and soon the rising sun, emerging from amidst golden and purple clouds, shed his blithesome rays on the tin weathercocks of Communipaw.

d.t: A feeling or appearance of optimism.
d.e: 1974, “April's Fading Carnation,” Time, 9 September, 1974,https://web.archive.org/web/20130813201436/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,904100,00.html The independence ceremony could not keep the blush of April's revolution, when carnations had seemed to sprout from…

d.t: A cosmetic, frequently a powder, used to redden the cheeks and lips.
d.e: The same rules that apply to face powder apply to powder blush, since neither contains water. Cream blush, however, should be replaced after a year. To prolong the life of any blush, clean your blush brush regularly and store the product in a dry place.

d.t: A color between pink and cream.
d.e: Makeup colors like ivory and blush dominate spring collections and have even infiltrated Burberry's shoes.

d.t: The collective noun for a group of boys.
d.e: a blush of boys

d.t: To become red or pink in the face (and sometimes experience an associated feeling of warmth), especially due to shyness, love, shame, excitement, or embarrassment.
d.e: The love scene made him blush to the roots of his hair / to the tips of his ears.

d.t: To be shy, ashamed, or embarrassed (to do something).
d.e: While Cato lives, Caesar will blush to see Mankind enslaved, and be ashamed of Empire.

d.t: To become red or pink.
d.e: The sun of heaven, methought, was loth to set, But stayed, and made the western welkin blush,

d.t: To suffuse with a blush; to redden; to pinken; to make rosy.
d.e: [the ghost] with the heart there cools and ne’er returneth To blush and beautify the cheek again.

d.t: To change skin color in the face (to a particular shade).
d.e: When he saw it, he blushed a beet red.

d.t: To express or make known by blushing.
d.e: Looking at me with a knowing glare, she blushed her discomfort with the situation.

d.t: To have a warm and delicate colour, like some roses and other flowers.
d.e: The garden was full of blossoms that blushed in myriad shades to form a beautiful carpet of color.

d.t: To glance with the eye, cast a glance.
One who blushes.
Face makeup that makes the cheeks rosier.
d.e: Beside him Lady Partridge, her head tilted up, her face a mask of blusher and brown powder, like someone just back from a skiing holiday, was also clearly elsewhere.

d.t: Any of several closely related, edible species of the genus Amanita, including Amanita rubescens and Amanita novinupta.
Embarrassment.
The act of one who blushes; a blush.
d.e: In observing the phenomena presented in a case of tubercular meningitis or acute hydrocephalus, one will scarce ever fail of noticing the repeated blushings or suffusions of face in the now insensible or lethargic patient.

d.t: Showing blushes; rosy red.
d.e: the blushing bride

d.t: Suffused with blushes or blushlike hues.
d.e: The artistic impulse that impels one to give a touch of beauty to all material objects extends even to the green-grocer and butcher, and the shop windows of these tradesmen betray both design and beanty. The blushiest side of the apple is always turned towards the passer-by and…

d.t: Embarrassed, blushing; feeling as though one might blush.
d.e: I didn't feel blushy or quakey, but quite cool, and only a little excited.

d.t: Pompous, officious talk.

d.t: A gust of wind.
Fitful noise and violence.
To speak or protest loudly.
d.e: When confronted by opposition his reaction was to bluster, which often cowed the meek.

d.t: To act or speak in an unduly threatening manner.
d.e: Your ministerial directors blustered like tragic tyrants.

d.t: To blow in strong or sudden gusts (refers to winds).
d.e: And ever-threatening storms / Of Chaos blustering round.

d.t: A noisy blowing, as of a blast of wind.
d.e: He will soon disregard the roaring of your eloquence, as the bold sailor contemns the blustering of the winds […]

d.t: Swaggering; braggartry; noisy pretension.
d.e: Boasting and blustering are as objectionable among nations as among individuals, and the public men of a great nation owe it to their sense of national self-respect to speak courteously of foreign powers just as a brave and self-respecting man treats all around him courteously.

d.t: Engaged in or involving the process of blustering, speaking or protesting loudly.
d.e: But when we began to renue our old acquaintance, and to shake the handes of discontinued familiaritie, alas, good Gentleman, his mandillion was ouercropped, his witt paunched like his wiues spindle, his art shanked like a lath, his conceit as lank as a shotten herring, and that…

d.t: Pompous or arrogant in one's speech or bearing.
d.e: The Old Inquirer, said Dick Honesty, in' visiting the sick, has seen too many bold, blustering Infidels, in this nasty condition, to entertain the smallest penchant either for their principles, or their exqusitely delightful exits.

d.t: Very windy; (of wind) blowing very strongly, blustery.
d.e: The southern wind Doth play the trumpet to his purposes, And by his hollow whistling in the leaves Foretells a tempest and a blustering day.

d.t: Blowing in loud and abrupt bursts.
d.e: Currently, there are blustery winds blowing in Patagonia.

d.t: Accompanied by strong wind.
d.e: Today is such a cold blustery day!

d.t: Pompous or arrogant, especially in one's speech; given to outbursts.
d.e: Duke Wilhelm […] seems to have been of a headlong, blustery, uncertain disposition; much tossed about in the controversies of his day.

d.t: Likeness; resemblance; look aspect; species; character.
d.e: I see a bly of your father about you.
